content: Herbal extracts are liquid solutions created by combining herbs with alcohol. The process involves mixing either dried or fresh herbs with alcohol, followed by the removal of the solid plant material, leaving behind the essential oils of the herbs dissolved in the alcohol. This method is known as extraction, which is why the resulting product is called an herbal extract. For instance, if peppermint is used in this process, the resulting product would be referred to as peppermint extract. Commercially available herbal extracts typically display a herb-to-alcohol ratio on their labels. When dried herbs are used, the standard ratio is often 1 part dried herb to 4 parts liquid, which consists of alcohol and water. In contrast, when fresh herbs are used, the most common ratio is 1:1. It is important to note that this ratio does not represent the quantity of the herb in the final product but rather the proportion of herb to liquid used during the extraction process. For example, a label indicating a dry herb strength of 1:4 signifies that the mixture used to create the extract consisted of 1 part dried herb and 4 parts liquid (alcohol and water). This ratio is distinct from the ingredients list, which is also typically provided on commercial extract labels. Herbal extracts are widely marketed as dietary supplements and are often utilized in alternative medicine practices. Additionally, they are commonly employed as flavoring agents in baking and cooking, similar to how vanilla extract is used. Among herbalists and practitioners of alternative medicine, herbal extracts are frequently referred to as tinctures.
